title: Lifecycle of a Spark SQL Query in a Fabric Notebook
purpose: Trace a %%sql/spark.sql() query from the notebook cell through Catalyst planning, AQE, the native-vs-JVM execution fork, to Delta reads and writes on OneLake.
accessibleSummary: A top-down internals flow with eight steps. A Spark SQL cell submits its query text to the same Spark session as any PySpark or Scala cell in the notebook. Catalyst parses and optimizes it into a physical plan, which Adaptive Query Execution can re-plan mid-run using runtime statistics. Each operator in that plan is then routed either to the Native Execution Engine's vectorized C++ path or, for unsupported operators, back to the standard JVM path, with the split visible per-operator in the Spark UI. Both paths read and write Delta tables in OneLake through the same Delta transaction log. A warning node calls out that native execution is not always bit-for-bit identical to JVM Spark for certain numeric operations.
longDescription: This is an internals diagram, not a pipeline: it explains what happens after a developer runs a %%sql cell in a Fabric notebook rather than how to build a data product. The query text enters the notebook's shared Apache Spark context — the same session backing PySpark, Scala, and SparkR cells — and is handed to Catalyst, Spark's query optimizer, which parses it and produces a logical then physical plan. Adaptive Query Execution can revise that physical plan mid-execution using statistics gathered from completed stages, for example switching join strategies once actual partition sizes are known. The physical plan's operators are then evaluated one by one against the Native Execution Engine: supported operators offload to a vectorized C++ path built on Velox and Gluten, while anything unsupported (structured streaming, ANSI SQL mode, some JSON/XML paths at time of writing) falls back per-operator to standard JVM Spark, so a single query can run partly native and partly JVM. Both paths converge on the same Delta read/write layer against OneLake, using the Delta transaction log for ACID guarantees. A dedicated warning node captures the specific, sourced risk that NEE is not always bit-for-bit identical to JVM Spark — decimal-to-float casting and round() are two documented divergence points — which matters for numerically sensitive pipelines.

nodes.label: %%sql / spark.sql() cell
nodes.summary: A Spark SQL query entered via the %%sql magic or spark.sql() call in a Fabric notebook.
nodes.detail: A Fabric notebook cell switched to Spark SQL via the %%sql language magic (or the cell language picker) submits its query text directly into the notebook's running Apache Spark context — the same session and cluster backing any PySpark, Scala, or SparkR cells in that notebook. There is no separate SQL service; the query is Spark SQL evaluated by the Spark engine itself.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because the query runs in the shared session, it inherits whatever lakehouse is pinned as default and whatever cluster resources the notebook already has — understanding this is the starting point for reasoning about everything downstream, including which metastore table names resolve against.

evidence.note: A %%sql cell executes its query as SparkSQL against the notebook's Apache Spark context, sharing the same running Spark session, cluster, and attached lakehouse as PySpark or Scala cells in that notebook.

inputs: Query text in a cell prefixed with %%sql, or a spark.sql("...") call in a PySpark cell
The notebook's pinned default lakehouse, which determines the metastore for unqualified table names
processing: Fabric routes the cell to the SparkSQL language runtime for that session
The query text is handed to the Spark SQL engine's parser as the entry point into Catalyst
outputs: A parsed query ready for Catalyst's logical planning phase
drill.example: A cell reading %%sql\nSELECT region, SUM(revenue) FROM sales GROUP BY region executes in the same session a prior PySpark cell used to read a DataFrame, with both sharing the notebook's attached lakehouse.
controls: Which lakehouse is pinned as the notebook's default
Session-level SQL behavior tuned via %%configure, e.g. livy.rsc.sql.num-rows controlling returned row count
failureModes: Querying a table in a lakehouse from a different workspace than the pinned default, which fails resolution because Spark SQL only resolves against the default lakehouse's metastore

nodes.label: Catalyst parse & logical plan
nodes.summary: Catalyst parses the query and builds an optimized logical plan.
nodes.detail: Catalyst, Spark's built-in query optimizer, parses the SQL text into an unresolved logical plan, resolves table and column references against the metastore, and applies rule-based optimizations (predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding) to produce an optimized logical plan. This stage is identical in shape to how Catalyst treats a DataFrame-API query — Spark SQL is not a separate optimizer path.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is where correctness and much of the baseline performance work happens before any physical execution decision is made; a query that is inefficient here stays inefficient regardless of native or JVM execution downstream.

inputs: Parsed query text from the SQL cell
Table/column metadata from the pinned lakehouse's metastore
processing: Resolve unresolved references against the metastore catalog
Apply rule-based logical optimizations: predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding
outputs: An optimized logical plan handed to the physical planner
drill.example: A query filtering WHERE region = 'EMEA' has that predicate pushed down past the GROUP BY in the logical plan, so downstream physical planning only ever considers EMEA rows.
controls: Standard Spark SQL conf settings that toggle specific Catalyst rules (e.g. constant folding, pushdown)
failureModes: Referencing a table not visible in the resolved metastore, producing a 'table not found' error at this stage rather than at physical execution

nodes.label: Physical planning with AQE
nodes.summary: The logical plan becomes a physical plan; Adaptive Query Execution can revise it mid-run.
nodes.detail: Catalyst's cost-based physical planner selects concrete execution strategies (join algorithm, shuffle partitioning) for the optimized logical plan. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) then re-optimizes parts of that physical plan during execution using runtime statistics gathered from completed shuffle stages — for example switching a sort-merge join to a broadcast join once actual partition sizes are known, or coalescing shuffle partitions. Fabric's Native Execution Engine explicitly preserves this AQE behavior even when some operators in the same query later offload to the native path.
nodes.whyItMatters: AQE is what keeps a single static plan from being wrong for the actual data at runtime; knowing it can still act on a partly-native query is important for reasoning about why an execution plan changed shape mid-run.

evidence.note: NEE preserves Fabric Spark's existing query optimizer behaviors — adaptive query execution, cost-based rewrites, column pruning, and predicate pushdown — so these still apply even to queries where some operators are offloaded to the native path and others fall back to the JVM.

inputs: The optimized logical plan from Catalyst
processing: Select initial physical operators and join strategies
Use post-shuffle statistics to re-plan remaining stages (join strategy switch, partition coalescing)
outputs: A physical plan, potentially revised mid-execution, ready for per-operator native/JVM routing
drill.example: A join initially planned as sort-merge is switched to a broadcast join by AQE once the shuffle stage reveals one side is small enough to broadcast, cutting shuffle volume for the rest of the query.
controls: AQE is enabled by default in Fabric Spark; specific thresholds (broadcast join size, partition coalescing) are tunable Spark SQL confs
failureModes: Disabling AQE for a workload that actually benefits from runtime re-planning, and then hand-tuning join strategies that AQE would have picked correctly

nodes.label: Native Execution Engine (Velox + Gluten)
nodes.summary: Supported operators run as vectorized, SIMD-accelerated C++ code instead of JVM bytecode.
nodes.detail: For operators the Native Execution Engine supports, Gluten intercepts the physical plan and converts the supported portion into a Substrait plan, which Velox — a C++ vectorized execution library — then runs as columnar, SIMD-accelerated native code in place of the JVM implementation. This is a per-operator decision within a single query, not an all-or-nothing switch.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the mechanism behind NEE's performance gain, and understanding it is per-operator (not per-query) explains why a query can show a mix of native and JVM operators in the same execution graph.

evidence.note: Gluten intercepts the optimized Spark SQL physical plan and converts supported portions into a Substrait plan, which Velox then executes as vectorized, SIMD-accelerated, columnar C++ code in place of JVM operator implementations.

inputs: Physical plan operators eligible for native execution
processing: Gluten converts the eligible plan segment into a Substrait representation
Velox executes that segment as vectorized columnar C++ code
Results flow back into the surrounding JVM-orchestrated query
outputs: Operator results computed on the native path, verifiable via Spark UI *Transformer suffixes or the Gluten SQL/DataFrame tab
drill.example: A filter-then-aggregate segment of the plan runs entirely through Velox; the Spark UI shows the corresponding operators suffixed *NativeFileScan and *VeloxColumnarToRowExec, and the Gluten tab colors those nodes green.
controls: NEE is opt-in per workspace/environment; whether it's enabled at all
failureModes: Assuming a query ran fully native without checking the Spark UI or Gluten tab, when in fact parts fell back to JVM

nodes.label: JVM Spark fallback
nodes.summary: Unsupported operators, expressions, or features execute on standard JVM Spark instead.
nodes.detail: When NEE encounters an operator, expression, data type, or feature it does not support, that segment of the query automatically falls back to standard JVM Spark rather than failing the job. Structured streaming and ANSI SQL mode always run on JVM Spark as of the current release; some JSON/XML source paths remain unaccelerated. Fabric Spark Advisor surfaces this fallback in real time as a cell-output alert.
nodes.whyItMatters: Fallback is what makes NEE safe to enable broadly — a query never fails because an operator is unsupported — but it also means performance gains are workload-dependent, not guaranteed for every query.

evidence.note: When NEE encounters an operator, expression, data type, or feature it doesn't support, the affected segment of the query automatically falls back to the standard JVM Spark engine rather than failing the job; Fabric Spark Advisor surfaces this fallback in real time in the cell output.
Structured streaming and ANSI SQL mode always execute on JVM Spark, and JSON/XML source formats are still not accelerated as of the current NEE release.

inputs: Physical plan operators NEE does not (yet) support
processing: Execute the unsupported segment on the standard JVM Spark engine
Fabric Spark Advisor posts a fallback alert in the notebook cell output
outputs: Correct results for the fallback segment, computed without native acceleration
drill.example: A structured-streaming query always falls back entirely to JVM Spark, regardless of whether NEE is enabled for the workspace, because streaming is out of scope for the native path at time of writing.
controls: Monitoring Spark Advisor's fallback alerts to identify which operators are worth rewriting or waiting on
failureModes: Treating a fully-fallback query as a NEE bug rather than checking whether it used an explicitly unsupported feature like structured streaming or ANSI SQL mode

nodes.label: Native results can diverge from JVM Spark
nodes.summary: NEE is not always bit-for-bit identical to vanilla Spark for certain numeric operations.
nodes.detail: Because Velox implements some operations independently rather than replicating JVM Spark's exact logic, documented divergences exist: DECIMAL-to-FLOAT casting differs because Velox casts directly from its internal int128_t representation instead of round-tripping through a string as Spark does, and round() can return different results because Velox uses the C++ standard library's std::round rather than Spark's own rounding logic. These are real, sourced discrepancies, not hypothetical edge cases.
nodes.whyItMatters: A pipeline that assumes native execution is a transparent, purely performance-only switch can silently produce different numeric results after enabling NEE — the kind of regression that surfaces as a data-quality dispute, not an error.

evidence.note: NEE casting from DECIMAL to FLOAT diverges from vanilla Spark: Spark preserves precision by round-tripping through a string conversion, while Velox casts directly from the internal int128_t representation, which can produce different rounding results for the same input.

The round() function can return different results under NEE than under vanilla Spark because Velox implements it using the C++ standard library's std::round rather than replicating Spark's own rounding logic.

inputs: A query that performs DECIMAL-to-FLOAT casts or round() calls and executes (at least partially) on the native path
processing: Identify which operators in the query are numerically sensitive
Test the same query with NEE enabled and disabled and diff results
Decide whether the divergence is acceptable or must be avoided for that pipeline
outputs: A documented decision on whether NEE is safe for that specific numerically sensitive query
drill.example: A financial rounding calculation using round() on currency values produces a one-cent discrepancy between NEE and JVM Spark for edge-case inputs, caught only because the team diffed results before shipping the pipeline to production.
controls: Test numerically sensitive pipelines with NEE both on and off before relying on it in production
Use the Spark UI or Gluten tab to confirm exactly which operators in a sensitive query ran natively
failureModes: Enabling NEE tenant-wide without auditing existing numerically sensitive pipelines for these specific divergence points
Discovering the discrepancy only via a downstream reconciliation or audit failure, long after the query shipped

nodes.label: Delta read/write on OneLake
nodes.summary: Both native and JVM paths converge on the same Delta transaction log against OneLake.
nodes.detail: Regardless of whether an operator executed natively or on JVM, table reads and writes ultimately go through the Delta transaction log against Delta tables stored in OneLake. NEE additionally supports parallel Delta snapshot loading and accelerates reads on Delta tables organized with Z-ordering or Liquid Clustering, giving further gains when the underlying data layout is optimized.
nodes.whyItMatters: This convergence point is why a partly-native, partly-JVM query still produces one consistent, ACID-safe result — the execution-engine split is purely a compute-layer optimization, not a storage-layer fork.

evidence.note: NEE supports parallel Delta snapshot loading and accelerates read operations on Delta tables organized with Z-ordering or Liquid Clustering, giving additional gains on top of raw operator vectorization when the underlying data layout is optimized.

inputs: Query results and write operations from both the native and JVM execution paths
processing: Resolve reads/writes against the Delta transaction log for the target table
Apply Z-order/Liquid-Clustering-aware parallel snapshot loading where the native path is engaged
outputs: Consistent, ACID-compliant Delta table state in OneLake, queryable by any engine
drill.example: A GROUP BY query that ran half-native, half-JVM still commits its output write through the same Delta log as any other Spark write, so the resulting table is indistinguishable from one written by a fully-JVM job.
controls: Z-ordering or Liquid Clustering on source tables, to get the additional NEE read acceleration
failureModes: Expecting NEE's read acceleration on a table with no Z-ordering or clustering applied, and being surprised the gain is smaller than benchmarked elsewhere

edges.label: query text into the shared Spark session

walkthrough.title: Start: a %%sql cell in the shared session
walkthrough.explanation: The query enters the same running Spark session as any PySpark or Scala cell in the notebook — there is no separate SQL service.

walkthrough.title: Catalyst parses and optimizes
walkthrough.explanation: Catalyst resolves references against the metastore and applies rule-based logical optimizations before any physical execution decision is made.

walkthrough.title: Physical planning, with room to change its mind
walkthrough.explanation: AQE can revise the physical plan mid-execution using runtime statistics — and keeps doing so even for queries that later split across native and JVM operators.

walkthrough.title: Branch: supported operators go native
walkthrough.explanation: Gluten converts eligible plan segments to Substrait; Velox executes them as vectorized C++ — this is a per-operator decision, not per-query.

walkthrough.title: Branch: unsupported operators fall back
walkthrough.explanation: Structured streaming, ANSI SQL mode, and some JSON/XML paths always run on JVM Spark, with Spark Advisor surfacing the fallback in the cell output.

walkthrough.title: Warning: native isn't always bit-identical
walkthrough.explanation: Documented divergences in DECIMAL-to-FLOAT casting and round() mean numerically sensitive pipelines should be tested with NEE on and off before trusting it in production.

walkthrough.title: End: both paths converge on Delta in OneLake
walkthrough.explanation: Native and JVM execution both read and write through the same Delta transaction log, so the compute-layer split never forks the storage-layer guarantees.
